key_insight: In thin 316L stainless-steel foils, increasing laser line energy triggers keyhole instability that nucleates holes, which then grow rapidly into perforations or cuts when their size approaches the sheet thickness.
engineering_relevance: The study provides a practical stability criterion and precursor signals for suppressing unwanted hole formation in laser welding of ultra-thin sheets and overlap joints.
method: High-speed imaging of laser keyhole welding on 100 μm 316L sheets, modeled as bead-on-plate welding of 200 μm foils.
Tracked the sequence from keyhole instability to hole nucleation and growth under increasing line energy.
Used a Young-Laplace-based force balance to interpret hole stability and growth behavior.
evidence_signal: Continuous seams were obtained up to about 7 kJ/m, hole formation began above this range, and cutting became dominant above about 12 kJ/m; hole growth occurred at roughly 0.8–1.2 m/s over 1–3 ms.
watch_item: The stability criterion is derived for very thin foils and may need revalidation for different alloys, thicknesses, joint geometries, or laser parameter windows.
paper_title: Rupture and growth of holes in the melt pool during laser keyhole welding of thin sheets
